A mosque and school in Fez, Morocco, founded in 857 or 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, the daughter of a rich merchant who had come from Kairouan in Tunisia. It is often called the oldest working university in the world.

It began as a neighbourhood mosque for migrants from Kairouan in the city of the Idrisid rulers. Over time it became a centre for teaching the Quran, Islamic law, grammar and later astronomy, mathematics and medicine. The Almoravids enlarged it in the 12th century, and the Marinid sultans built colleges around it. Its library holds very old manuscripts and was restored in 2016.

Scholars linked to it include Ibn Khaldun, and tradition says the Jewish thinker Maimonides studied in Fez. Teaching was centred on religion for most of its history. It joined Morocco's state university system in 1963. Along with Al-Azhar in Cairo, it shows how mosque schools became the great centres of learning in the Muslim world.
